Programmable design of functional proteins from natural language

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Programming biological function—designing bespoke proteins to perform specified molecular tasks—is a foundational goal of molecular engineering. However, current design models remain fundamentally limited1,2,3: they typically require either natural proteins as starting points for optimization or manual reformulation of functional goals as geometric and sequence-level constraints to guide candidate generation. Here we introduce Pinal, a 16-billion-parameter foundation model that designs candidate proteins from natural-language descriptions of desired function. Trained on 1.7 billion synthetically annotated protein–text pairs, Pinal links functional intent to protein sequence and structure. In computational evaluations, generated candidates combined high predicted foldability with functional-description alignment and sequence diversity, providing a basis for prioritizing experimentally testable designs. We applied Pinal to four distinct design tasks—a fluorescent protein, a polyethylene terephthalate hydrolase, an alcohol dehydrogenase and a metabolic H-protein—and experimentally observed the intended function in each case, including catalytic activity for both designed enzymes. Without iterative experimental optimization, a Pinal-designed H-protein increased product titre by 1.7-fold relative to the corresponding native Escherichia coli H-protein in a multi-enzyme CO2 fixation pathway. These findings support natural language as a high-level interface for candidate generation in protein design, enabling programmable exploration with reduced reliance on manually specified structural or sequence constraints.

Protein sequences were obtained from UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot and UniProtKB/TrEMBL (https://www.uniprot.org/, release 2023_03). Predicted protein structures were obtained from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/). Functional annotations and keywords were obtained from InterPro (version 101.0; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/), and enzyme classification information was obtained from the ENZYME nomenclature database (https://enzyme.expasy.org/). Experimentally determined protein structures used for structural comparisons were obtained from the Protein Data Bank (PDB; https://www.rcsb.org/). UniRef100 (https://www.uniprot.org/help/uniref) was used for sequence-similarity analyses. Fluorescent-protein reference information was obtained from FPbase (https://www.fpbase.org/). The pretrained Pinal weights can be downloaded from https://huggingface.co/westlake-repl/Pinal. All the other data are available within the paper and the Supplementary Information. Source data are provided with this paper.

Pinal is open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 license. The code repository is available at GitHub (https://github.com/westlake-repl/Denovo-Pinal). The Pinal web server is located at http://www.denovo-pinal.com/. The SaProt-T/O server, corresponding to the second component of Pinal, is linked from the Pinal web server and can also be accessed directly at http://113.45.254.183:9527/. The release of large-scale training resources for generative protein design requires careful consideration of potential dual-use biosecurity risks. In developing Pinal, the large-scale structural component of the training corpus was derived from AFDB, whose released protein-structure collection does not include viral proteomes. Accordingly, Pinal was not trained or intended for viral protein design. Nevertheless, unrestricted public release of the full pretraining corpus together with the complete training pipeline could lower the barrier for adapting similar systems to sensitive biological datasets. To mitigate this risk, these full-scale training resources were provided only under confidential access for editorial and peer review assessment. Because they will not be publicly released in full, and to support transparency and reproducibility, we instead provide public access to the inference code, evaluation code, model usage instructions, trained model weights and the web server, in line with common release practices for large-scale protein foundation models such as AlphaFold69,74, ESM338 and ESMFold68. Additional information about the composition, sources, filtering strategy, and construction of the training corpus is provided in the Methods and Supplementary Information.

a: T2struct translates natural language descriptions into structural (3Di) token sequences. A text encoder first generates the text representation according to the function prompt. This representation is then used to guide the T2struct decoder block, which autoregressively predicts the sequence of 3Di structural tokens. The detailed view (right) illustrates the internal composition of each decoder block (repeated N times), consisting of three sequential sub-modules: a structural context module (implemented via multi-head self-attention) to process the generated structural sequence, a text-conditioning module (employing multi-head cross-attention) to integrate guidance from the text representation, and a feature refinement network (a pointwise feed-forward layer) for further feature processing. Layer normalization is applied within each sub-module. b: The SaProt-T module, which designs an amino acid sequence based on both the structural input and the text prompt. A semantic projector maps the text representation into the same embedding space as the structural tokens. This projected text vector is prepended to the structural token embeddings to form a text-protein joint representation. This joint representation is then processed by the SaProt-T block, repeated N times, to predict the final amino acid sequence.

a: Ablation study comparing the performance of SaProt-T and SaProt-O (760M parameters) against the original SaProt (650M), the ProstT5 baseline, and the scaled SaProt-T-T5xxl_encoder (~5B). Performance is evaluated based on textual alignment (x-axis) and predicted foldability (y-axis). The results show that our text-conditioned models (SaProt-T/O) outperform the original SaProt and the ProstT5 baseline, particularly in maintaining structural foldability. The size of each bubble corresponds to the number of model parameters, as indicated in the legend. b: Composition of the omni-modal training strategy for the SaProt-O model. This strategy involves a varied combination of masking applied to the amino acid (AA) sequence, the structural tokens, and the text prompt to train a flexible, multi-purpose design model. The left panel details the distribution of structural token masking (no, partial, or full masking) under two different AA masking conditions. The right panel shows that the text prompt is masked in 40% of the training examples.

Performance of the top-ranked Pinal designs on the “hard” test set as a function of the number of sampled candidates (K). For each value of K, we generate K candidates, rank them by their joint log-probability, and then evaluate the top-ranked design. Left panel: textual alignment, measured by Max. and Mean Seq. ProTrek score. Right panel: predicted structural plausibility, measured by ESMFold pLDDT. Both textual alignment and foldability improve as K increases from 5 to 50. Further increasing K to 100 yields only marginal gains (or a slight decrease in ProTrek score) while substantially increasing computational cost. Based on this analysis, K = 50 is used as the standard setting for all experiments, offering a robust balance between design performance and inference efficiency.

The figure validates the ProTrek score’s performance using a test set of 1,000 protein-text pairs from Swiss-Prot. The top row (a-c) evaluates the text-to-sequence score (Seq. ProTrek), while the bottom row (d-f) evaluates the text-to-structure score (Struc. ProTrek). (a, d) Box plots show the distribution of ProTrek scores for proteins paired with their original descriptions, LLM-paraphrased descriptions, and randomly assigned (mismatched) descriptions. For both sequence and structure, the scores for original and paraphrased text are high and similar, while scores for random text are lower, demonstrating the metric’s discriminative power. Box plots show the median (centre line), 25th-75th percentiles (box), the most extreme values within 1.5 × the interquartile range (whiskers), and outliers (points). (b, e) Scatter plots comparing the scores of original versus paraphrased descriptions for each protein. The strong linear relationship, confirmed by a Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient (ρ) of > 0.98 for both sequence and structure, demonstrates that the metric is robust to variations in wording and captures core semantic meaning. (c, f) Scatter plots comparing the scores of original versus randomly assigned descriptions. The near-zero correlations (ρ ≈ 0) further confirm that the ProTrek score is a valid metric that reliably distinguishes between relevant and irrelevant protein-text pairings. The original ProTrek study also demonstrated that its score selectively responds to biologically relevant keywords while ignoring non-functional terms. Building on this capability, a recent benchmark paper48 adopted ProTrek as a key metric for evaluating the alignment between protein sequences and their textual descriptions.

a, Performance of the 15.5B T2struct model on the “hard” test set across three distinct training phases. Phase 1 (320k steps) represents initial training; Phase 2 (625k steps) incorporates data filtering by ProTrek score; Phase 3 (740k steps) is a final fine-tuning step on higher-quality data filtered to exclude low-pLDDT scores and high token repetition. The plots demonstrate that the third phase improves protein foldability, while incurring only a minor, acceptable trade-off in textual alignment (ProTrek score). b, Analysis of the sequence repetition phenomenon that motivated the third training phase. The left panel shows that the model after Phase 2 exhibited a high rate of amino acid repetition (≥5) (e.g.,“AAAAA”) at 60.2%, far exceeding that of natural proteins (UniProt, 4.0%). The final model after Phase 3 substantially reduces this rate to 35.3%. The right panel illustrates the effectiveness of the Phase 3 training data-filtering strategy. The high rate of Foldseek token repetition in the Phase 2 model’s outputs (91%) correlates with the high rate found in the AFDB training data (90%). The refined training strategy after Phase 3 successfully reduces the rate of token repetition greater than 10 to just 4%, thereby substantially resolving the Foldseek structure token repetition issue.

The figure evaluates Pinal’s design performance across 17 distinct functional categories curated from Swiss-Prot. Left panel: Analysis of textual alignment, measured by the maximum sequence ProTrek score (n = 50 functional prompts per subsection). The performance of Pinal’s top-ranked design (blue) is compared against a random baseline (light grey) and the ground-truth protein (dark grey) for each category. Pinal consistently outperforms the random baseline across all categories and approaches ground-truth performance, demonstrating robust language understanding. Right panel: Predicted structural plausibility of the corresponding Pinal-designed proteins, measured by ESMFold pLDDT (n = 250 Pinal-designed proteins per subsection). The results indicate that Pinal generates proteins with high predicted foldability (median pLDDT is typically > 80) across all functional description types, from concrete categories like “Protein names” to more abstract ones like “Disruption phenotype”. Box plots show the median (centre line), 25th-75th percentiles (box), the most extreme values within 1.5 × the interquartile range (whiskers), and outliers (points).

a, Flowchart illustrating the multi-tiered computational filtering strategy applied to the initial Pinal-generated sequences. This pipeline culminated in the selection of 29 candidates for experimental validation. b, Multiple sequence alignment of pinalGFP, avGFP, and esmGFP-b8. The alignment highlights the substantial sequence divergence of pinalGFP from both the natural protein and the other synthetic variant. c, Normalized fluorescence excitation (dashed lines, λem = 510 nm) and emission (solid lines, λex = 460 nm) spectra of pinalGFP (blue) and avGFP (green). d, Size-exclusion chromatography profiles of purified GFP variants on a Superdex 200 column. Elution volumes reflected their oligomeric states in solution: avGFP was predominantly dimeric, whereas pinalGFP exhibited a more complex profile dominated by higher-order multimers.

a, Flowchart illustrating the multi-tiered screening strategy used to identify the active PETase candidate from the initial pool of Pinal-generated sequences. Candidates were first filtered on the basis of predicted structural quality (ESMFold pLDDT  > 80, PAE  < 7) and text–protein alignment (ProTrek score  > 15), yielding 2,416 sequences. The top 94 candidates, ranked by ProTrek score, were then subjected to esterase activity screening using the p-nitrophenyl butyrate (pNPB) assay. This workflow led to the identification of a single standout variant, pinalPETase36, which was subsequently advanced to PET hydrolysis validation. The inset shows the predicted active-site architecture of pinalPETase36. b, Standard curve for p-nitrophenol (pNP) used for quantification of esterase activity in the pNPB assay. Absorbance at 410 nm was plotted against pNP concentration, showing a strong linear relationship (R2 = 0.9947). Data are shown as mean  ± s.d. (n = 3 independent measurements).

a, Flowchart of the computational screening and selection process for ADH candidates. From an initial library of 2,500 generated sequences, 1,639 candidates passing the feasibility filters based on structural confidence (ESMFold pLDDT  > 80, PAE  < 7) were identified, from which 1,000 sequences were randomly retained for downstream prioritization. From these, eight diverse candidates representing different ADH subfamilies were selected, leading to five successfully validated enzymes. b, UMAP of alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) sequences. A total of 1,000 Pinal-designed ADH sequences (blue) were analysed together with natural ADH sequences from Swiss-Prot (gray; EC 1.1.1.1). Sequence embeddings were generated using ESM2-650M and projected into two dimensions by UMAP. The Pinal-designed sequences span a substantial region of the natural ADH sequence space. c, Representative HPLC chromatograms of derivatized acetaldehyde standards, corresponding to the product of the ADH-catalyzed reaction. Acetaldehyde standards at 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5 mM showed a consistent retention time of approximately 7.3 min.

a, Flowchart illustrating the computational design and screening pipeline for H-protein candidates. The initial generation was filtered to yield approximately 1,000 sequences that simultaneously satisfied the protein-text alignment criterion (ProTrek score > 15) and the sequence-divergence criterion ( < 60% sequence identity to known homologs). From this pool, 20 highly ranked candidates were selected, identifying five sequences with experimentally confirmed activity. b, Initial activity screening of 14 soluble Pinal-designed H-proteins compared to the native E. coli H-protein (‘ecH’). Glycine synthesis was measured after a 2 h reaction in a reconstituted Glycine Cleavage System (GCS). Data are shown as mean  ± s.d. (n = 3 biologically independent reactions). c-f, Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations comparing the conformational dynamics of the lipoamide arm in the top-performing ‘pinalH02’ and the native ‘ecH’. c, Trajectory of the distance between the Cδ atom of Glu27 in ‘pinalH02’ and the nitrogen atom of the lipoamide arm over 500 ns. The plot shows that the arm frequently samples extended conformations far from the protein core. d, Corresponding distance trajectory for ‘ecH’, plotting the distance between the Cδ atom of Glu12 and the arm’s nitrogen atom over 500 ns. The arm remains stably sequestered close to the protein body. e, A representative snapshot of the ‘pinalH02’ conformation at 200 ns, illustrating the solvent-exposed lipoamide arm. f, A representative snapshot of ‘ecH’ at 200 ns, showing the aminomethyl lipoate arm locked within the protein’s hydrophobic cavity.

GRP75-dependent SIMPA mediates inter-organellar quality control

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Mitochondria are bound by a double membrane and are semiautonomous organelles, rendering them highly vulnerable to global and internal proteostatic stress1. Multiple surveillance mechanisms at proteostatic and inter-organellar levels have evolved to maintain mitochondrial integrity and cellular health2,3,4,5,6,7. However, the precise mechanisms by which proteostatic damage relays stress signals across organelles and how the quality surveillance machinery coordinates these functions remain unknown. Here we report that under proteostatic stress, damaged mitochondrial proteins are sequestered to form stress-induced mitochondrial protein aggregates (SIMPAs) that activate specific quality control mechanisms in a spatially confined manner without perturbing the mitochondrial network. Quantitative proteomic and correlative light–electron microscopy analysis revealed that SIMPA mediates inter-organellar communication via mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes. Mechanistically, GRP75 coordinates SIMPA biogenesis and focally activates endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response pathways via mitochondria–endoplasmic reticulum contact sites or mitochondrial-associated membranes for the targeted clearance of SIMPAs. Functionally, in both cellular and liver disease models, we found that a GRP75-dependent SIMPA signalling cascade attenuates mitochondrial stress and preserves mitochondrial integrity under proteotoxic stress. Overall, we show that SIMPAs, functioning as protein condensates, serve as a central cross-compartment communication hub for mitochondrial quality control, supporting cellular and organismal fitness.

Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses

📅 Oct 26, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.

Hantaviruses are a large and globally distributed family of viruses associated with severe zoonotic disease in humans. The New World hantaviruses (NWHs) ANDV and Sin Nombre virus (SNV) cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in South and North America, respectively, with high case-fatality rates that can approach 40%. Cardiogenic shock and respiratory failure are hallmarks of HCPS. Old World hantaviruses (OWHs) are endemic in Europe and Asia or globally distributed in some cases (Seoul virus (SEOV)). The OWH Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) are associated with severe zoonotic disease and considerable mortality. Although hantaviruses are typically transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, ANDV appears uniquely capable of human-to-human transmission2,3, raising its global public health significance and epidemic potential. This risk was underscored by the recent ANDV outbreak on a cruise ship departing Ushuaia, Argentina4. No US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- or European Medicines Agency (EMA)-approved medical countermeasures are available to prevent or treat hantaviral infections.

Hantavirus glycoprotein spikes are formed by two glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which are organized into a partial lattice at the surface of the virion. Each spike consists of four Gn molecules that form a central stabilizing core surrounded by four Gc molecules at the periphery. Gc mediates the interspike contacts that stabilize the lattice. Gn consists of a head (GnH) and a base (GnB) domain. GnH is exposed at the viral surface and is thought to participate in receptor binding, whereas GnB is buried within the spike and mediates most of the intraspike interactions. Gc consists of three domains that drive membrane fusion. At neutral pH, GnH interacts with Gc, forming a pre-fusion complex that prevents premature fusion. After exposure to acidic pH, the Gn–Gc complex dissociates, allowing Gc to insert three hydrophobic loops into the host cell membrane and undergo conformational rearrangements that drive fusion of viral and cellular membranes. Structural studies have reported the structures of GnH, GnB, Gc, the GnH–Gc complex and the Gn–Gc spike from several hantaviruses5,6,7,8,9,10.

Understanding how hantaviruses recognize their cellular receptors is a critical step toward the rational development of therapies and vaccines. Previous studies have identified several cell-surface molecules as candidate entry host factors, including integrins β1–3 (refs. 11,12,13,14), decay accelerating factor (DAF, encoded by CD55)15,16, complement factors (gC1qR)17 and the cadherin-superfamily protein PCDH1 (ref. 1). However, only PCDH1 has been shown to directly recognize the ANDV Gn–Gc spike1,18 and to be required for infection of human endothelial cells—major targets of hantavirus infection1,19. Furthermore, PCDH1 is critical for ANDV infection in vivo and for disease pathogenesis in a lethal hamster model of ANDV challenge1,18. PCDH1 is a type I membrane protein expressed in human airway epithelial and endothelial cells. It contains seven extracellular cadherin-repeat (EC) domains that extend into the extracellular space. Binding studies have shown that PCDH1 does not recognize soluble monomeric glycoproteins but instead binds to the tetrameric glycoprotein spikes displayed on the viral surface1,18. Monoclonal antibodies targeting the first EC repeat (EC1) inhibited entry of a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) pseudotyped with Gn–Gc from multiple NWHs1, and point mutations at the tip of EC1 prevented PCDH1’s interaction with Gn–Gc of rVSVs bearing the glycoproteins of ANDV (rVSV-ANDV)1,18. Together, these findings indicate that NWHs infect host cells by engaging the EC1 domain of PCDH1. However, the structural determinants of this interaction remain unclear. Here we sought to determine the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV Gn–Gc spike.

PCDH1 binds to viral particles but not to the soluble GnH–Gc heterodimer1,18, suggesting that the receptor-binding site is presented only on viral spikes. To elucidate the structural basis for PCDH1 recognition, we designed a soluble version of the ANDV spike tetramer by adding a hetero-octamerization domain at the C-terminal end of the Gn and Gc ectodomains (Fig. 1a). The octamerization sequence was derived from HALC4_136, a de novo tetramerization domain comprising three antiparallel helices per protomer20. We split this scaffold by fusing the first two helices to Gn and the third helix to Gc, so that co-expression of Gn and Gc would reconstitute a hetero-oligomeric assembly with the stoichiometry of the native spike (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We cloned both genes into a bicistronic plasmid, purified the complex from the supernatants of stably transfected Drosophila melanogaster S2 cells using affinity and size-exclusion chromatography and confirmed that it interacts with a truncated PCDH1 construct consisting of wild-type EC domains 1 to 4 (sEC1–4WT) using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA; Fig. 1b). As a negative control, we used a construct containing the substitutions Y81A and F83A (sEC1–4MUT), which are known to abrogate virus binding18. We also confirmed that incubation of the soluble spike with an excess of soluble sEC1WT, but not sEC1MUT, prevented the binding to sEC1–4WT (Fig. 1c). Furthermore, we used biolayer interferometry (BLI) to demonstrate specific spike–EC1 binding. Specifically, sEC1–4WT or sEC1–4MUT were immobilized on sensors, which were then dipped into solutions containing increasing concentrations of soluble spike (Fig. 1d). BLI assays performed in the opposite orientation corroborated these findings (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

To verify that the soluble spike proteins fold like the spikes observed on the viral surface, we performed cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). We observed a few two-dimensional (2D) classes compatible with Gn–Gc tetramers (Extended Data Fig. 1c). However, a low-resolution three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction obtained from them was not compatible with the known ANDV spike structure5 (Extended Data Fig. 1d), suggesting that, in the absence of lateral contacts between spikes and the transmembrane regions, the intersubunit contacts within the spike are not sufficiently stable to maintain the intact eight-subunit assembly. We next hypothesized that prolonged incubation of the two proteins might help to stabilize the spike in its receptor-binding conformation. To test this hypothesis, we co-transfected S2 cells with the plasmids encoding sEC1–4WT and the soluble spike and purified the complex using double-affinity and size-exclusion chromatography. We performed cryo-EM studies and observed many new 2D classes showing tetramers (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Extended Data Table 1). Using particles from these classes, we reconstructed a map at a resolution of 2.4 Å, and we used the map to build a model of the spike that closely resembles the tetramers observed on viral particles5. The only notable differences between the two models are a slight rotation of the GnH domains relative to GnB and the poorly resolved density for domain III in the soluble spikes (Extended Data Fig. 3).

The cryo-EM map of the complex revealed an additional density at the centre of the spike, consistent in size with a single EC domain of PCDH1. However, as the map was processed using C4 symmetry, and the symmetry axis passes through the centre of the spike, we were unable to model this residual density. We reprocessed the map by combining a masked 3D classification with a non-uniform refinement using a pseudo-C4 symmetry. This approach yielded a new map at a resolution of 2.6 Å (Fig. 1e), in which we modelled PCDH1 EC1 at the centre of the spike (Fig. 1f,g). The final model showed the EC1 domain deeply inserted into a pocket formed by four protomers of Gn, establishing contacts with two neighbouring protomers (660 and 200 Å2, respectively) and sparse contacts with the other two (80 Å2 and 35 Å2). This mode of interaction, whereby one receptor molecule interacts with four viral glycoproteins, represents a binding mode that to our knowledge has not been observed in any enveloped virus, and explains why PCDH1 binds to viral particles but not to soluble GnH–Gc heterodimers. In the model, EC1 loops BCEC1 and FGEC1 interact with the AB and CD loops of GnH and the DE loop of GnB from two neighbouring protomers (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Notably, the densities corresponding to the DE and CD loops are weaker in the protomers that do not engage EC1 than in the receptor-contacting protomers (Extended Data Fig. 3b). This suggests that these loops are flexible and that PCDH1 binding stabilizes specific conformations of these regions. Indeed, comparison of the four protomers reveals that EC1 binding induces a conformational change in the CD and DE loops of one protomer, creating asymmetry within the pocket (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Previous studies have identified PCDH1 mutations that inhibit virus binding18, and all are in the BCEC1 loop or nearby regions, probably altering the conformation of the loop. Consistent with the structural data, mutations in the tip of the FG loop had little (D142A, D142R) or no (L143A, V144A, Q145A) effect on virus binding18, probably because none of them introduce steric restrictions (Fig. 1g).

To validate the model with viral particles, we studied the interaction between PCDH1 and virus-like particles (VLPs). We did not attempt to decorate preformed VLPs with soluble receptor because flow cytometry revealed only weak binding of EC1 to ANDV glycoproteins presented on the cell surface. Instead, reasoning that increasing the local concentration of receptor near the spike could enhance binding, we fused EC1 to the N terminus of the M segment through a flexible linker (Fig. 1a). To increase particle production, we introduced an EABR tag21 and the V535K and S1096L mutations, as reported previously5,22, and transfected the construct into FreeStyle293 cells. We analysed the secreted particles using cryo-EM and obtained a reconstruction of the spike at an overall resolution of 3.9 Å (Extended Data Fig. 5). The map revealed clear densities for Gn and Gc and an additional density at the centre of the spike (Fig. 1h). This central density was compatible in size and position with the PCDH1 EC1 domain observed in the soluble spike complex. However, the quality of this density did not allow unambiguous building of the EC1 domain, preventing a detailed comparison of the VLP–receptor interface with that obtained using the soluble spike (Extended Data Fig. 5c). This work nevertheless confirmed that PCDH1 EC1 occupies the central region of the Gn–Gc tetramer in viral particles.

To begin to investigate the roles of the CD and AB loops of GnH and the DE loop of GnB in spike–PCDH1 recognition, we produced rVSV-ANDV and rVSVs bearing the glycoproteins of the PCDH1-independent1,19 OWH HTNV (rVSV-HTNV), as well as rVSV-ANDV variants in which we replaced the GnH CD loop or all three loops in contact with the receptor (Methods and Extended Data Fig. 4a) with those from HTNV. After normalizing the amount of incorporated Gn–Gc in the viral particles (Extended Data Fig. 4b), we measured their interaction with immobilized PCDH1 EC1 on ELISA plates. Consistent with the known receptor specificity of hantaviruses and our structural data, PCDH1 EC1 could capture rVSV-ANDV but not rVSV-HTNV or any of the chimeric variants (Fig. 2a).

Next, we used a deep-mutational scanning (DMS) approach to more comprehensively survey the sequence landscape of the spike–PCDH1 interaction. We generated two independent Gn libraries, each introducing all possible amino acid substitutions at 427 of 448 positions in the ectodomain (amino acids 24–471; Methods) and used these to create libraries of alphavirus-based vectors pseudotyped with ANDV Gn–Gc (Sem-Hantavirus (SHV)). We captured SHVs bound to PCDH1 EC1 immobilized on ELISA plates and sequenced the PCDH1-bound SHV fractions to identify variants enriched or depleted relative to the input population. We observed strong selective signals for the GnH CD and AB loops and nearby regions in both populations, consistent with roles for these sequences in virus–receptor recognition (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 6). Relatively few variants were recovered from the GnB DE loop, consistent with its higher level of conservation (Extended Data Fig. 4a) and suggesting an important structural role for this sequence in the assembly and/or stability of the spike. Notably, none of the Gn ectodomain substitutions observed in the recent Hondius outbreak isolate of ANDV (LS-CH2016/2016-12-23/Switzerland) mapped to the PCDH1-binding pocket or were selected in the DMS experiments, indicating that this virus probably resembles previous isolates of the virus in its ability to recognize and use PCDH1 (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 6).

PCDH1 is a specific receptor for NWHs, and we wondered whether the structure of the complex could reveal insights into receptor use. We analysed the sequence conservation of the PCDH1-binding pocket across hantaviruses and compared the conformation of the loops using the available crystal structures of HTNV and SNV. We identified two amino acid substitutions: one in the GnH AB loop of SEOV, DOBV and HTNV (L36F) and one in the GnB DE loop of HTNV (G418L) that are predicted to cause steric clashes with PCDH1. By contrast, both the sequence and structure of the GnH CD loop vary substantially across hantaviruses—it is an extended loop in NWHs but a compact helix in OWHs (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4). These findings suggest that it is not only the residues directly contacting PCDH1 that are important to the spike–receptor interaction but also nearby residues that influence the overall conformation of the loops, as is also indicated by the DMS data (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 6).
